title: What happens when you call a @Transactional method
summary: From your call site to the database transaction, and back. Read invokeWithinTransaction and getTransaction and you have read most of Spring's transaction support.
entry: Put a breakpoint on the first line of your own @Transactional method, run a test that calls it, and read the frames below yours. That stack is this list.

steps.notice: You are inside the proxy, not your object. Nothing here is reached when one method of your bean calls another directly, which is the whole explanation of why self-invocation loses the transaction.
The generic interceptor chain. It walks a list and calls proceed() again each time, so the same frame appears once per advice. Transactions, caching, retry and security all queue up here.
Almost nothing happens here. It delegates straight to the superclass, which is a good early lesson in Spring: the class named after the feature is often just the adapter.
The whole feature, in one method. Begin, invoke, commit on success, roll back on the exceptions the rules say are rollback-worthy. Worth reading top to bottom before anything else.
Where the TransactionAttribute (your @Transactional settings, already parsed) meets the transaction manager.
The decision point for propagation. Read this and then handleExistingTransaction and you know all seven modes; everything else about propagation is commentary.
Only runs when a transaction is already in progress. REQUIRES_NEW suspends, NESTED makes a savepoint, MANDATORY is happy, NEVER throws. One switch statement is the entire propagation matrix.

The thread-local that makes it all work. The Connection is bound here, which is why the transaction does not follow you onto an @Async thread and why @TransactionalEventListener hangs its callbacks off this.
The rollback rules. By default only RuntimeException and Error roll back, so a checked exception commits. Set a breakpoint here once and you will never be surprised by that again.
